research_question: Does widening the dependence premise of the aseity-to-simplicity argument to include constitutive or grounding dependence successfully rule out the possibility of a metaphysically composite yet self-existent necessary being?

argument.title: God cannot be a composite
argument.paper_title: Simple is as simple does: Plantinga and Ghazālī on divine simplicity

premises.text: Divine simplicity is the claim that God is not a composite of more basic features.
premises.quote: the notion of divine simplicity, the idea that God is not a composite of more basic features

premises.text: It is contradictory for something to exist both through itself and through another.

missing_premise.text: God is not causally dependent on his distinct properties, either efficiently or as final causes.

conclusion.text: Therefore, the Necessary Existent (God) cannot be a composite; consequently, God’s existence is simple.

challenged_premise.text: If God were not simple, he would depend on properties like power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes.

objection: Consider the necessary being called the Foundation. The Foundation is essentially composed of three irreducible perfections: potency, knowledge, and bliss. These are really distinct features, so the Foundation is not simple. Nevertheless, the Foundation exists through itself; its existence is absolutely necessary and not teleologically ordered toward these perfections. The three perfections are not final causes—they are not ends for the sake of which the Foundation exists—but are co-eternal constituents or necessary formal aspects of its nature. The Foundation does not depend on them as goals to be realized; rather, it simply has them necessarily as part of what it is. Therefore, a being can be composite with distinct properties without depending on those properties as final causes.

strongest_responses.response: Defender A widened the dependence premise to include constitutive or grounding dependence, arguing that a whole whose existence through itself requires really distinct constituents is posterior to its parts and therefore lacks full aseity.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: Defender A conceded that the original conditional in c012 is false because the objector's stipulated Foundation is not teleologically ordered toward its perfections, and admitted that the incompatibility between constitutive dependence and aseity had not been established in the exchange.

strongest_responses.response: Defender B recast the threat of non-simplicity as dependence on distinct metaphysical constituents that ground the being's nature, proposing that if God were not simple he would depend on distinct properties as constituents and therefore would not exist wholly through himself.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: The objector's Foundation was explicitly introduced as a being with really distinct formal aspects and no final-cause dependence, so Defender B's shift to grounding dependence restates the disputed claim rather than answering the counterexample.

open_questions: Is constitutive dependence on distinct necessary properties genuinely incompatible with aseity, or can a being exist through itself while having really distinct metaphysical constituents?
Does the revised argument against composition covertly beg the question by defining aseity in a way that presupposes the impossibility of distinct metaphysical parts?
Can the traditional distinction between abstract perfections as formal aspects of a simple being and as distinct entities be defended without already assuming divine simplicity?
What principled criterion distinguishes a composite necessary being with irreducible perfections from a simple being signified under different formal aspects?
paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the inference from divine aseity to absolute simplicity cannot be repaired simply by widening the dependence premise to include constitutive or grounding dependence, because the objector's model of a necessarily self-existent yet metaphysically composite being demonstrates that really distinct constituents need not function as causes—efficient, final, or grounding—of the whole's existence. The case would develop the Foundation thought experiment to distinguish between constituents that ground a nature and causes on which a being depends, and would press the question of whether existing through oneself is compatible with having irreducible metaphysical parts. The strongest reply to anticipate is the defender's claim that any real distinction among perfections amounts to a form of grounding dependence that compromises aseity, effectively treating composition as sufficient for ontological dependence. To succeed, the paper would need to show either that the concept of a composite yet absolutely independent necessary being is internally incoherent, or that the defender's widened dependence premise begs the question by defining aseity in a way that excludes complexity rather than demonstrating its incompatibility.

reasons.coherence: The objection does hit c012 as worded, since it targets final-cause dependence specifically. But the paper plan names 'show that a composite yet independent necessary being is incoherent' as one way to succeed, which would vindicate the defender rather than the thesis, so the direction is confused about its own aim.
reasons.robustness: The Foundation case wins only by stipulating away grounding dependence, and neither the case nor the transcript offers a principled reply to the composition-requires-a-unifier or parts-prior-to-whole principles. A competent referee would press these first.
reasons.significance: Showing that c012's final-cause version is too narrow is easy and already conceded in the literature. Showing that widening to grounding dependence begs the question is a well-worn move, so success would be at most a modest refinement unless it supplied a new model of non-dependent composition.
reasons.specificity: There is a recognizable thesis and a test case, but the plan offers a disjunctive and partly incoherent success condition and no concrete account of grounding, parthood, or aseity to deploy, so a writer would not yet know what to argue in each section.

assessment.strongest_objection: The Foundation is a stipulation, not an argument. Declaring that three really distinct perfections are 'co-eternal constituents' on which the whole does not depend assumes the very point at issue. The defender's standard principles go unaddressed. One is the Thomistic claim that any composite needs a ground of its composition, something that makes these distinct items one being. The other is the mereological claim that a whole is posterior to its proper parts. So the counterexample defeats only the narrow final-cause wording of c012, a premise the literature already treats as a strawman of the aseity argument (Plantinga 1980; Brower; Pruss; Schmid; Mullins). It leaves the real grounding-based argument untouched.
assessment.what_it_needs: It must give an independent, non-stipulative account of how really distinct necessary constituents can belong to a whole without being prior to it, for example a whole-priority (Schaffer-style) model or a non-grounding account of essential parthood, and answer the 'cause of composition' principle directly. It should also drop the self-undermining success condition of proving composite necessary beings incoherent, and engage the existing aseity/grounding literature on divine complexity.
assessment.summary: The objection rightly exposes the narrowness of the final-cause premise, but as a paper it rests on a stipulated counterexample that does not engage the grounding-and-composition principles defenders actually use, so it would need a substantive positive model of non-dependent composition before it is worth writing.

revision.research_question: If the dependence premise of the aseity-to-simplicity argument is widened to cover grounding dependence on distinct constituents, does that rule out a necessary being that exists through itself yet has really distinct parts, once we settle whether a whole is prior to or posterior to its parts?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the aseity-to-simplicity inference does not go through merely by widening the dependence premise from final causation to constitutive or grounding dependence. The argument would be narrowed to a conditional claim. Whether a composite necessary being is ruled out depends on a further thesis about the priority relation between a whole and its proper parts. Under parts-priority, where the whole is grounded in its parts, a composite Foundation would depend on its perfections and aseity would be violated, so the widened premise does its work. Under whole-priority, where the whole is prior and the parts depend on the whole, the Foundation's constituents do not ground its existence, and the widened premise is not triggered. The paper would not rely on the Foundation as a stipulated counterexample. Instead it would take the two principles the referee presses, that composition requires a ground of composition and that a whole is posterior to its proper parts, and test each. For the unifier principle, the paper would ask whether the ground of composition must be distinct from the whole. If the unifying ground can be the being itself, then the principle yields no dependence on anything other than the whole, and the defender needs an extra premise to get dependence on something distinct. The paper would argue that this extra premise is what the aseity argument requires, and that it is not supplied by aseity alone. It would also drop the success condition of proving composite necessary beings incoherent, since that would vindicate the defender. The contribution would be a precise statement of what the widened premise needs in order to yield simplicity, with a whole-priority model of essential parthood as the test case, and an engagement with the existing literature on aseity and divine complexity.
revision.reply_to_strongest_objection: The referee is right that the Foundation case, taken alone, stipulates that its perfections are non-grounding constituents, so the paper does not rest on it. The reply has three parts. First, the paper accepts that the final-cause version of c012 is too narrow and concedes that point. Second, it does not assume that composition yields no dependence; it asks which priority relation holds between the whole and its parts, and it shows that the answer decides whether widened dependence applies. Third, it answers the unifier principle directly: a ground of composition establishes dependence on something distinct only if that ground is not the whole itself. If it is the whole, aseity is intact. The paper's claim is that aseity plus widened dependence does not entail simplicity without this further premise, and that the defender has to supply it.
revision.what_changed: The direction now narrows the thesis to a conditional claim about whole-priority and parts-priority, replaces the stipulated Foundation with a test of the referee's unifier and parts-posterior principles, and drops the self-undermining incoherence success condition.

reasons.coherence: The original objection squarely hits c012's final-cause wording, but the paper moves to a widened premise the argument never states, and its claim that the whole can be its own ground of composition sits uneasily with talk of really distinct co-eternal constituents.
reasons.robustness: Its main move, conditioning the verdict on parts-priority versus whole-priority, overlooks that the traditional argument uses existential or modal dependence on essential parts, which survives whole-priority, and neither the plan nor the transcript answers this.
reasons.significance: A precise account of what extra premise turns aseity plus widened dependence into simplicity would be a useful refinement, but the existing literature on divine complexity (Mullins, Schmid, Brower, Pruss) already presses close variants of this point.
reasons.specificity: It gives a definite conditional thesis, a test model (whole-priority essential parthood), and two principles to examine, though the whole-priority model is not actually specified and the literature engagement is only gestured at.

assessment.strongest_objection: The classical aseity argument (Avicenna, Ghazālī, Aquinas) does not turn on grounding priority but on need or existential dependence: a whole whose really distinct parts are essential to it cannot exist unless each part exists, and no part is identical to the whole. The whole therefore exists 'through another' whichever way the grounding arrow runs. Whole-priority does not block this dependence. Worse, a whole-priority model on which the 'distinct' perfections are merely aspects grounded in the undivided whole looks like the simplicist's own view of one being signified under different formal aspects, so the dispute becomes verbal.
assessment.what_it_needs: The paper must show that the defender's relevant notion of dependence (Avicennan iftiqār, or modal-existential dependence on essential proper parts) is either reducible to grounding or illegitimately strong, so that the priority question really decides the case. It must also show that its whole-priority model yields a composite being genuinely distinct from the simplicist's formal-aspects view, not a relabelling of it.
assessment.summary: A tidy diagnostic thesis, but as planned it attacks a grounding version of the dependence premise that the classical defender need not hold, so the first referee will ask why essential-part existential dependence is not enough for violated aseity, and the proposal has no answer yet.
